newsitem.title: JAPAN: Will MOF's Sakakibara remain Japan's Mr Yen?.
newsitem.headline: Will MOF's Sakakibara remain Japan's Mr Yen?.

text.p: Like so many comments by currency market pundits, the answer is maybe yes, maybe no.

Eisuke Sakakibara, Japan's newly appointed vice finance minster for international affairs, will retain his influence on dollar/yen exchange rates, but the man the markets call "Mr Yen" may find his power slightly tempered after his promotion.
"He will remain a key figure for the dollar/yen market," said the general manager of a major U.S. bank in Tokyo.
"But his influence may become less omnipotent as the market heads towards an age of turbulence," he added.

Though now one of Japan's top bureaucrats, Sakakibara, formerly director of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, may find it tougher to exercise his power over the yen exchange rate, traders in Tokyo said.

At a time when the formerly unthinkable -- such as a leap by the dollar to 2.0000 marks and a nosedive by Asian currencies across the region -- seem nearer reality, the possibility for one person to influence the global exchange market seem smaller.
Other traders pointed to Sakakibara's unusual style favouring active involvement in the market, both publicly and behind the scenes.

"His style of thoroughly researching market conditions and having frequent communication and interaction with market participants is valuable as a market regulator," said a chief currency trader at a Japanese bank.
But if he overdoes this it could eventually turn into a major source of market volatility, which official regulators would then need to rein in, he added.

Sakakibara earned the nickname "Mr Yen" for his ability to sway currency markets with a single comment, and has been credited with spearheading a drive to counter the yen's steep rise in 1995 with financial market liberalisation steps.
